heroIntro: Sea-borne trade through Chattogram, Mongla, and Payra ports frequently sparks urgent disputes over short-landed or damaged cargo, unpaid charter hire, bunker fuel supply, crew wages, or vessel collisions. Under the Admiralty Court Act 2000, the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh exercises exclusive original admiralty jurisdiction—empowering claimants to obtain an immediate warrant of ship arrest in rem within hours before a vessel sails out of territorial waters.

quickAnswer.heading: At a Glance: Maritime & Ship Arrest Law in Bangladesh
quickAnswer.text: Only the High Court Division has original admiralty jurisdiction to arrest ships in Bangladeshi ports.

sections.h2: Exclusive Admiralty Jurisdiction of the High Court Division
sections.content: Unlike ordinary money suits filed in District Courts, maritime claims fall exclusively before the designated Admiralty Bench of the High Court Division under Section 3(1) of the Admiralty Court Act 2000. Subordinate civil courts lack jurisdiction to entertain an action in rem against a ship or order port detention of sea-going vessels at Chattogram, Mongla, Payra, or Matarbari.

sections.h2: Grounds for Arresting a Vessel Under Section 3(2) of the 2000 Act
sections.content:
Under Section 3(2), a claimant can invoke admiralty jurisdiction against a vessel if the claim falls within the 18 enumerated maritime heads—whether the claim arose inside Bangladesh or on the high seas:

  • Cargo Damage & Bill of Lading Claims: Short delivery, contamination, or damage to goods carried into or out of Bangladeshi ports under a Bill of Lading or charterparty.
  • Supply of Necessaries & Bunkers: Unpaid marine fuel, provisions, spares, or ship repairs furnished to the vessel.
  • Charterparty, Demurrage & Collision: Disputes arising out of time/voyage charter agreements, vessel collision, towage, pilotage, or salvage.
  • Crew Wages & Ship Mortgages: Master and crew claims for unpaid wages or enforcement of registered maritime mortgages.

sections.h2: Step-by-Step Procedure to File an Admiralty Suit & Arrest a Ship
sections.content:
Because a commercial vessel typically stays at outer anchorage or jetty for only 24 to 72 hours, admiralty filings are moved on an urgent basis:

  1. Ad Valorem Court Fee & Verified Plaint: Prepare the Admiralty Plaint supported by affidavit, original Bills of Lading, Lloyd’s/port survey reports, commercial invoices, and customs short-landing certificates, paying court fees under Schedule Rules.
  2. Ex Parte Motion for Warrant of Arrest (Section 4): Move an urgent application before the Admiralty Judge seeking a Warrant of Arrest against the defendant vessel in rem.
  3. Marshal & Port Authority Execution: Once granted, the High Court Marshal immediately transmits the arrest warrant via urgent notice to the Chattogram or Mongla Port Authority, Mercantile Marine Department, and Customs to withhold Port Clearance until further order.

sections.h2: Releasing an Arrested Vessel: Bank Guarantee vs. P&I Club LOU
sections.content:
Vessel owners losing tens of thousands of dollars per day in detention charges seek immediate release once an arrest warrant is served:

  • Security Deposit / Bank Guarantee: Under High Court Admiralty Practice, a ship is released immediately once the owner furnishes a cash deposit or unconditional Bangladeshi Scheduled Bank Guarantee covering the suit claim plus estimated interest and costs.
  • P&I Club Letter of Undertaking (LOU): Protection & Indemnity (P&I) Clubs frequently propose an LOU; however, unless the plaintiff expressly consents in writing to accept an LOU from a recognized International Group P&I Club, Bangladeshi Admiralty Courts normally insist on local bank guarantee or cash security.

sections.h2: Time Bar, Cargo Short-Landing Proofs & Sister-Ship Arrest Rules
sections.content:
Maritime litigants must guard against strict statutory limitation periods and evidentiary traps:

  • One-Year Hague/Carriage Rule vs. Limitation Act: Cargo claims under bills of lading incorporating Hague/Hague-Visby Rules often carry a 1-year time bar unless extended by agreement, whereas general maritime contracts follow the Limitation Act 1908.
  • Sister-Ship Arrest (Section 4(4)): Under Section 4(4), if the offending vessel has already sailed, a claimant may arrest a sister ship beneficially owned by the exact same shipowner at the time the action is brought.
  • Joint Survey Documentation: Before unloading clears port premises, consignees must secure joint stevedore/surveyor reports and Customs Outturn Reports; without contemporaneous tally proofs, carrier defenses under inherent vice or perils of the sea prevail.

faqs.q: How fast can a ship be arrested at Chattogram Port through the High Court?
faqs.a: When all supporting bills of lading, survey reports, and court-fee chalans are ready, an urgent admiralty motion can be moved and the arrest order communicated to Chattogram Port Authority within the same working day.

faqs.q: Can I arrest a vessel if the Charterparty has a London or Singapore arbitration clause?
faqs.a: Yes, claimants often file an action in rem in Bangladesh to obtain security for a maritime claim; however, defendants may apply to stay merits proceedings in favor of contractual foreign arbitration while keeping furnished security intact or contested depending on High Court orders.

faqs.q: Who bears port charges while a ship remains under High Court arrest?
faqs.a: Ordinarily the shipowner remains responsible for port dues, crew maintenance, and anchorage expenses; if the owner abandons the vessel, the court may order judicial auction under Section 6 and distribute sale proceeds by maritime priority.
